claims.text: Local fluctuations in chemical ordering, particularly at nanoparticle surfaces, control the onset of premelting and melting.
Surface regions enriched in lower-melting-point constituents initiate surface melting at lower temperatures than uniformly composed regions.
Melting initiated in chemically enriched surface regions propagates into the nanoparticle core.
Surface chemical fluctuations lower the particle's overall melting transition relative to a uniformly ordered baseline.
The initial Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles are solid, chemically homogeneous, and single-phase solid solutions.
The proposed comparison deliberately varies surface chemical ordering while maintaining a uniformly distributed control group.
The proposed simulations span temperatures from below to above melting, use ambient pressure, and examine particles 5-50 nm in size.
Copper is an example of a lower-melting-point constituent that can enrich localized surface regions.
Chemically distinct surface domains reduce the energy barrier for atomic mobility.
The reduced barrier for atomic mobility initiates localized premelting.
Localized surface premelting promotes growth of the liquid phase into the nanoparticle interior.
Growth of the surface-initiated liquid phase into the interior decreases the overall melting temperature relative to a particle with homogeneous surface composition.
Nanoparticles with enhanced surface chemical heterogeneity will exhibit an earlier onset of surface melting than uniformly distributed controls.
Nanoparticles with enhanced surface chemical heterogeneity will have a lower effective melting point than uniformly distributed controls.
The proposed mechanism applies to pristine, nonoxidized, defect-free nanoparticles in the 5-50 nm size range under conditions capable of resolving spatially varying melting.
The magnitude of the melting-temperature shift and the spatial extent of premelting strongly depend on the chosen interatomic potentials and simulation parameters.
Failure of enhanced surface heterogeneity to produce a statistically significant change in melting onset or progression relative to the uniform control would falsify the hypothesis.
